newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil up on Colombian crude cut, trade buying.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil up on Colombian crude cut, trade buying.

text.p: Oil prices jumped a half a dollar on Monday despite news that the United Nations had removed the last major obstacle to a resumption of limited Iraqi crude exports.
U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan formally approved a revised aid distribution plan submitted by Baghdad, clearing the way for the first Iraqi crude exports since late May.
London September futures for bellwether North Sea Brent blend shot upwards in late trade to end the day 50 cents stronger at $19.45 a barrel.
Brokers attributed the price rise to the closure of a Colombian crude oil field and to dealers buying after the Iraqi news in order to balance their books.
"Everyone went short and expected to cover themselves once the distribution plan was agreed. But when they came to the market there were just other buyers there," one said.

Reports of the shut in of an average 175,000 barrels per day of Colombian crude supplies after the country's main pipeline was blown up twice and partially destroyed by a landslide at the weekend saw U.S. dealers coming out to buy, pushing prices higher.
Dealers said technical problems at three gasoline producing units in northwest Europe also fueled fears of even scarcer supplies just as holidaymakers push demand to its seasonal peak.

"With implied (gasoline) demand in the U.S. so strong and shipments from Europe and elsewhere needed during the peak demand period, this is the kind of news that leaves the bulls feeling rather pleased," said brokers GNI.
But analysts said the prospect of Iraq's return was bound to work through to the market in the medium-term.

"Once the August demand peak passes, rising supply will be the dominant force affecting price dynamics. Iraq will exacerbate an already oversupplied crude market," said Washington-based consultants Petroleum Finance Company in a report.
Traders said Iraqi crude could be flowing again from the Mina al Bakr terminal in the Gulf and the Turkish port of Ceyhan in a matter of days, once pricing formulas and contracts have been agreed.

Under the terms of the U.N. deal implemented last December, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in two 90-day periods of $1 billion each to raise money for food and medicine.
The deal was renewed on June 8 but Iraq refused to export any more oil until the U.N. agreed to a streamlined aid distribution plan, depriving world markets of some 600,000 barrels per day of crude.
The fall in crude supply coincided with a surge in U.S. gasoline demand which inflated refinery operating rates by a similar amount compared with year-ago levels.
Prices responded by touching a six-week high of $19.09 a barrel on July 31 but despite Monday's rise, with extra crude coming on the market, prices were heading in only one direction, analysts said.

Traders say Iraq looks set to push as much as 1.4 million bpd to buyers in a short burst in an effort to meet the billion-dollar target it is permitted in the next tranche of the agreement which expires in early September.
Even so, lean global stocks should prevent crude prices going into an immediate tailspin, they said.

Mehdi Varzi at research house Kleinwort Benson said he had reduced his estimate for the global build in oil stocks during the second quarter by 700,000 barrels a day (bpd) to 1.5 million. His forecast for the third quarter had been cut by 200,000 bpd to 1.6 million
"Inventories have grown at a much slower rate so far this year than originally feared," said Varzi.
"If you look at the stockbuild during the period of Iraq's absence and compare it with what was expected you have a totally different fundamental picture," a European oil trader said.
